newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Pressure mounts on Africans to discard Boutros.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts on Africans to discard Boutros.

text.p: Pressure was increasing on African states on Friday to end their defiance of a U.S. veto against Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali and come up with other candidates for the post.

So far the Security Council, which met on the issue on Friday, has been deadlocked since Nov. 19 when the United States cast the sole negative vote in the 15-member body. Boutros-Ghali's five year term expires on Dec. 31.

Members, however, said they were asking Cameroon, which holds the presidency of the Organisation of African Unity, to decide soon if states would stick to Boutros-Ghali in light of the U.S. veto or submit other names. The message would be delivered to Cameroon's U.N. delegation.

The council previously agreed to give priority to candidates from Africa on the grounds that if Boutros-Ghali is denied the second term given to his predecessors, he should at least be followed by another African.

But Botswana's U.N. ambassador, a council member, told reporters that "the most dangerous thing you can do is elect a secretary-general in a hurry. We have said that consultations are taking place on the African continent among 53 countries. And you don't expect them to consult in one week, or agree."
Security Council President Nugroho Wisnumurti of Indonesia told reporters, "I understand the African countries require sufficient time to do so, because they are 53."
But, he said, "There are other members of the United Nations that really are waiting and now they are getting impatient about this process."
"To reflect the feeling of other council members, to reflect the feeling of the general membership of the United Nations, I decided to continue to prod our African brothers, gently," Wisnumurti said.

He said the council had three options: to wait until the Organisation of Africa Unity was ready with a list; to open the door for individual Africans to submit names while waiting for the OAU, and to open the door for non-African states to submit the name of an African candidate.
Wisnumurti will be replaced as council president on Monday by Francesco Paulo Fulci of Italy, whose government is pushing for a compromise of keeping Boutros-Ghali in office for about two years.
Diplomats said Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi wrote President Bill Clinton a letter two weeks ago urging a compromise, but had received no reply.

Previously, French President Jacques Chirac, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien and Indonesian President Suharto all wrote to Clinton in early November asking him to change his mind on Boutros-Ghali. It was not known if they received a reply or if they mentioned a compromise.
But U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright said such a deal was out of the question.
"The United States position has been very clear from the very beginning," she said. "We have said we need a new secretary-general and it is our position that no compromise formula is acceptable."

Behind the scenes the contest appears to be turning into an Anglo-French poker game. France has made it clear that if Boutros-Ghali has no chance it wants a "francophone," presumed to mean an African from a French-speaking country.

So far the only francophone name on an informal list is Amara Essy, the Ivory Coast's foreign minister who served as president of the General Assembly in 1994-1995. But he spoke little English during his stay in New York, including taking an interpreter to informal lunches with journalists.
Therefore, diplomats believe a summit between France and African states, mainly francophone, in the Burkina Faso capital of Ougadougou on Dec. 5 may be crucial in revealing Paris' hand.

Five members of the council have veto power: the United States, Russia, China, France and Britain. The other 10 members who rotate for two year periods, five each year, are: Botswana, Chile, Egypt, Germany, Guinea-Bissau, Honduras, Indonesia, Italy, South Korea and Poland.
